[1] DORA, Article 22: Supervisory feedback
1. Without prejudice to the technical input, advice or remedies and subsequent follow-up which may be provided, where applicable, in accordance with national law, by the CSIRTs under Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the competent authority shall, upon receipt of the initial notification and of each report as referred to in Article 19(4), acknowledge receipt and may, where feasible, provide in a timely manner relevant and proportionate feedback or high-level guidance to the financial entity, in particular by making available any relevant anonymised information and intelligence on similar threats, and may discuss remedies applied at the level of the financial entity and ways to minimise and mitigate adverse impact across the financial sector. Without prejudice to the supervisory feedback received, financial entities shall remain fully responsible for the handling and for consequences of the ICT-related incidents reported pursuant to Article 19(1).
2. The ESAs shall, through the Joint Committee, on an anonymised and aggregated basis, report yearly on major ICT-related incidents, the details of which shall be provided by competent authorities in accordance with Article 19(6), setting out at least the number of major ICT-related incidents, their nature and their impact on the operations of financial entities or clients, remedial actions taken and costs incurred.
The ESAs shall issue warnings and produce high-level statistics to support ICT threat and vulnerability assessments.

[2] AMLR, Article 54: Coexistence of ownership interest and control in the ownership structure
Where corporate entities are owned through a multi-layered ownership structure, and in one or more chains of that structure the ownership interest and the control coexist in relation to different layers of the chain, the beneficial owners shall be:
(a) the natural persons who control, directly or indirectly, through ownership interest or via other means, legal entities that have a direct ownership interest in the corporate entity, whether individually or cumulatively;
(a)
the natural persons who control, directly or indirectly, through ownership interest or via other means, legal entities that have a direct ownership interest in the corporate entity, whether individually or cumulatively;
(b) the natural persons who, whether individually or cumulatively, directly or indirectly, have an ownership interest in the corporate entity that controls, through ownership interest or via other means, the corporate entity, directly or indirectly.
(b)
the natural persons who, whether individually or cumulatively, directly or indirectly, have an ownership interest in the corporate entity that controls, through ownership interest or via other means, the corporate entity, directly or indirectly.

[3] PSD2, Article 19(2): Use of agents, branches or entities to which activities are outsourced
2. Within 2 months of receipt of the information referred to in paragraph 1, the competent authority of the home Member State shall communicate to the payment institution whether the agent has been entered in the register provided for in Article 14. Upon entry in the register, the agent may commence providing payment services.

[4] AI Act, Article 57(4): AI regulatory sandboxes
4. Member States shall ensure that the competent authorities referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 allocate sufficient resources to comply with this Article effectively and in a timely manner. Where appropriate, national competent authorities shall cooperate with other relevant authorities, and may allow for the involvement of other actors within the AI ecosystem. This Article shall not affect other regulatory sandboxes established under Union or national law. Member States shall ensure an appropriate level of cooperation between the authorities supervising those other sandboxes and the national competent authorities.

[5] AI Act, Article 2(5): Scope
5. This Regulation shall not affect the application of the provisions on the liability of providers of intermediary services as set out in Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065.

When onboarding a new financial institution that operates as a legal entity similar to an express trust, how do we verify that the beneficial ownership information is accessible through a public central register, and what specific details must be included in the notification we submit to the Commission by 10 October 2027?

To verify that beneficial ownership information is accessible through a public central register, we must confirm that the legal entity is included in a central register and that the process for accessing such information is publicly available, as required under [AMLR, Article 57(3)]. The notification submitted to the Commission by 10 October 2027 must include a description of the form and basic features of the legal entity, the process through which it can be set up, the process for accessing basic and beneficial ownership information, and the websites at which the central registers can be consulted along with the contact details of the entities in charge of those registers [AMLR, Article 57(3)]. Additionally, the notification must include a justification explaining why the legal entity is considered similar to an express trust and why other legal arrangements under national law are not considered similar [AMLR, Article 57(3)].

1. The Board shall act independently when performing its tasks or exercising its powers pursuant to Articles 70 and 71.
2. Without prejudice to requests by the Commission referred to in point (b) of Article 70(1) and in Article 70(2), the Board shall, in the performance of its tasks or the exercise of its powers, neither seek nor take instructions from anybody.

[3] GDPR, Article 52: Independence
1. Each supervisory authority shall act with complete independence in performing its tasks and exercising its powers in accordance with this Regulation.
2. The member or members of each supervisory authority shall, in the performance of their tasks and exercise of their powers in accordance with this Regulation, remain free from external influence, whether direct or indirect, and shall neither seek nor take instructions from anybody.
3. Member or members of each supervisory authority shall refrain from any action incompatible with their duties and shall not, during their term of office, engage in any incompatible occupation, whether gainful or not.
4. 5. Each Member State shall ensure that each supervisory authority chooses and has its own staff which shall be subject to the exclusive direction of the member or members of the supervisory authority concerned.
6. Each Member State shall ensure that each supervisory authority is subject to financial control which does not affect its independence and that it has separate, public annual budgets, which may be part of the overall state or national budget.

(a) where, in a case referred to in Article 60(4), a supervisory authority concerned has raised a relevant and reasoned objection to a draft decision of the lead authority or the lead authority has rejected such an objection as being not relevant or reasoned. In the event that a senior executive at our firm requests that we provide a recommendation on a regulatory decision that involves a potential conflict of interest, how should we ensure that our Board's decisions remain independent and do not inadvertently receive instructions from internal stakeholders or external parties?

The Board shall act independently when performing its tasks or exercising its powers pursuant to Articles 70 and 71, and shall neither seek nor take instructions from anybody [GDPR, Article 69]. Each supervisory authority shall remain free from external influence, whether direct or indirect, and shall neither seek nor take instructions from anybody [GDPR, Article 52]. To ensure independence, the Board must not receive instructions from internal stakeholders or external parties, including senior executives, when making decisions on regulatory matters [GDPR, Article 52]. This independence is fundamental to the Board’s role and must be maintained throughout the decision-making process [GDPR, Article 52].

What steps must a trading platform take by 31 December 2027 to comply with the requirement for a crypto-asset white paper, and how should it ensure the white paper is updated in line with new developments or regulatory expectations?

A trading platform must ensure by 31 December 2027 that a crypto-asset white paper is drawn up, notified, and published in accordance with Articles 6, 8, and 9 of MiCA, and that it is updated in accordance with Article 12 [MiCA, Article 143(2)]. When there is a significant new factor, material mistake, or material inaccuracy that affects the assessment of the crypto-asset, the platform must modify the white paper and, where applicable, its marketing communications [MiCA, Article 12(1)]. Upon modification, the platform must immediately inform the public on its website of the notification of the modified white paper and provide a summary of the reasons for the modification [MiCA, Article 12(3)].

In a scenario where a fintech firm receives a request from a national authority to provide metadata related to customer communications, and the request requires a court order under national law, should our firm proactively apply for such a court authorisation—even if the request is not yet formally made—based on the principle of precaution?

Yes, the fintech firm should proactively apply for such a court authorisation even if the request is not yet formally made, based on the principle of precaution. This is because, under MiCA, Article 123(5), EBA shall apply for such authorisation when a request for records of telephone or data traffic requires authorisation from a court pursuant to applicable national law, and such authorisation may also be applied for as a precautionary measure. [MiCA, Article 123(5)]

If a delegated regulation is notified to both the European Parliament and the Council, and the European Parliament expresses an objection within the 3-month period, does the regulation still enter into force, and what steps must the Commission take to ensure the regulation is validly implemented?

No, the regulation does not enter into force if the European Parliament expresses an objection within the 3-month period, as it must be objected to by either the European Parliament or the Council for the regulation to be blocked from entering into force [DORA, Article 57]. The Commission must ensure the regulation is validly implemented only if both the European Parliament and the Council have informed the Commission that they will not object, or if no objection is expressed within the 3-month period, which may be extended by three months at the initiative of either institution [DORA, Article 57]. Additionally, before adopting a delegated act, the Commission must consult experts designated by each Member State in accordance with the Interinstitutional Agreement of 13 April 2016 on Better Law-Making [DORA, Article 57]. The Commission must also notify the regulation simultaneously to both the European Parliament and the Council upon adoption [DORA, Article 57].

If we are transferring personal data from a country outside the EU to a third country, and that third country does not have adequate data protection laws, we must implement appropriate safeguards as required by [GDPR, Article 46(1)]. If a cybersecurity incident occurs that compromises the integrity of our customer data stored in a cloud-based system, how should we ensure that our technical and organisational measures meet the required level of security under this rule, especially given the nature of real-time financial transactions and the potential impact on users’ rights?

To ensure that technical and organisational measures meet the required level of security, controllers and processors must implement appropriate measures taking into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation, and the nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing, as well as the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons [GDPR, Article 32(1)]. Given the nature of real-time financial transactions and the potential impact on users’ rights, pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data are specifically required to protect the integrity and confidentiality of customer data [GDPR, Article 32(1)]. Furthermore, financial entities must establish a sound network and infrastructure management structure, including automated mechanisms to isolate affected information assets in the event of cyber-attacks, to mitigate risks to data integrity and availability [DORA, Article 9(4)]. They must also implement strong authentication mechanisms and protection measures for cryptographic keys, based on approved data classification and ICT risk assessments, to ensure data integrity and secure access [DORA, Article 9(4)]. Additionally, regular testing, assessment, and evaluation of technical and organisational measures are necessary to ensure ongoing effectiveness in protecting data integrity, especially in high-risk financial environments [GDPR, Article 32(1)].

We should notify the competent authorities of our jurisdiction, as they are responsible for ensuring compliance with consumer protection rules, particularly in cases involving branches established within their territory [PSD2, Article 29(1)]. These authorities must then communicate, upon request, all relevant information about the suspected violation, including details on the compliance of the payment institution with the conditions under Article 11(3) [PSD2, Article 29(3)]. Furthermore, the competent authorities of our jurisdiction must cooperate with the competent authorities of the host Member State, including notifying them of any intended on-site inspection, and may delegate such inspections to the host authorities if appropriate [PSD2, Article 29(1)]. This cooperation ensures that the information-sharing obligations are met under the framework of the regulation [PSD2, Article 29(1)].

The German-headquartered payment institution must appoint a central contact point in France to ensure adequate communication and information reporting on compliance with Titles III and IV of PSD2, as required by [PSD2, Article 29(4)]. This central contact point must be capable of ensuring compliance with applicable law on behalf of the institution, in accordance with [AMLR, Article 8(6)]. The institution must also ensure that the central contact point is designated and operational in France, as the agent operates under the right of establishment and freedom to provide services [PSD2, Article 29(4)]. Furthermore, the German institution must communicate the agent’s details, internal control mechanisms, and management personnel to the competent authorities in Germany, as required under [PSD2, Article 19(1)]. This communication supports the overall compliance framework and enables effective supervision by both German and French authorities.

The custodian must act honestly, fairly, professionally, independently, and in the interest of the issuers of the asset-referenced tokens and the holders of such tokens [MiCA, Article 37(8)]. The issuer of the asset-referenced token must ensure that the custodian has the necessary expertise and market reputation, and that contractual arrangements protect the reserve assets from claims of the custodian’s creditors [MiCA, Article 37(4)]. If the misrepresentation affects the value, stability, or risks of the token or its reserve assets, the issuer must put in place mechanisms to protect holders and take appropriate corrective measures to address concerns related to market integrity or financial stability [MiCA, Article 25(4)]. The issuer must also properly identify, monitor, manage, and disclose any potential conflicts of interest to holders, in accordance with Article 32 [MiCA, Article 37(9)].

In the case of a fintech firm managing a reserve of assets tied to asset-referenced tokens, how would we identify and disclose a conflict of interest if one of the company's executives also holds a financial interest in a third party that is a beneficiary of the token's underlying asset performance?

A conflict of interest arises when an executive of a fintech firm managing a reserve of assets tied to asset-referenced tokens holds a financial interest in a third party that benefits from the performance of the underlying asset. Such a conflict must be identified, monitored, managed, and disclosed by the issuer to the holders of the asset-referenced tokens in accordance with Article 32. The issuer is required to implement effective policies and procedures to identify, prevent, manage, and disclose conflicts of interest between themselves and their shareholders, members, employees, or any third party providing functions under Article 34(5)(h), including such executive interests [MiCA, Article 32(1)]. Furthermore, the issuer must ensure that such conflicts are properly disclosed to holders of the asset-referenced tokens as part of their obligations under Article 32(2) and Article 32(1)(e) [MiCA, Article 32(2)]. The disclosure must be made in a manner that ensures transparency and allows holders to understand the potential impact on their interests [MiCA, Article 32(1)].

Upon receiving a notification from a potential acquisition of an issuer of an asset-referenced token, the competent authority shall promptly acknowledge receipt thereof in writing, and in any event within two working days following receipt of the notification [MiCA, Article 41(3)]. This acknowledgment must be provided in writing to ensure compliance with the timeline [MiCA, Article 41(3)]. If a fintech firm is found to have failed to cooperate with a regulatory investigation, what specific administrative measures could be imposed under this rule, and what steps should the firm take to avoid such penalties?

Failure to cooperate with a regulatory investigation constitutes an infringement covered by Article 111(1)(f) of MiCA, which authorises competent authorities to impose administrative penalties and other administrative measures [MiCA, Article 111(1)]. Such measures may include issuing an order requiring the firm to cease non-compliant conduct and desist from repetition, as provided under Article 50(4)(a) of DORA [DORA, Article 50(4)]. To avoid such penalties, the firm should promptly respond to any regulatory request, provide full and accurate information, and cooperate fully with investigations as required by law [DORA, Article 50(4)].

When our systems are disrupted—say, during a cyberattack that takes down our payment processing platform—do we need to ensure that all relevant transaction and user activity logs are preserved and accessible in real time, even during the recovery phase, and how long must those records remain available for audit or regulatory review?

When systems are disrupted, financial entities shall keep readily accessible records of activities before and during disruption events when their ICT business continuity plans and ICT response and recovery plans are activated [DORA, Article 11(8)]. These records must be maintained to ensure data integrity during recovery, including when reconstructing data from external stakeholders [DORA, Article 12(7)]. However, the sources do not specify the duration for which such records must remain available for audit or regulatory review.

If we transfer personal data to a country that is covered by an adequacy decision, under what conditions does that decision remain valid and continue to apply to our data transfers, and what should we do if we become aware that the decision might be at risk of being revoked or replaced?

If we transfer personal data to a country that is covered by an adequacy decision, that decision remains valid and continues to apply to our data transfers until it is amended, replaced, or repealed by a Commission Decision adopted in accordance with the relevant provisions of the GDPR [GDPR, Article 45(9)]. Under such circumstances, the adequacy decision provides a legal basis for data transfers without requiring specific authorisation [GDPR, Article 45(1)]. If we become aware that the decision might be at risk of being revoked or replaced, we should monitor official updates from the European Commission and remain vigilant about any developments that could affect the validity of the adequacy decision [GDPR, Article 45(9)]. We should also ensure that our data processing activities are compliant with the current status of the adequacy decision and, if necessary, adjust our practices accordingly. Additionally, we must inform the supervisory authority of any significant changes in the data transfer arrangements, especially if the adequacy decision is no longer in force [GDPR, Article 49(1)].

This retention period applies to data processed for the purpose of investigation, inspection, or other supervisory duties under the regulation [DORA, Article 56]. The retention period may be extended if, on a case-by-case basis, the necessity and proportionality of further retention have been established for the prevention, detection, investigation, or prosecution of suspected money laundering or terrorist financing, as specified in [AMLR, Article 77(1)]. Such extension is permitted only where the data is relevant to ongoing legal proceedings and is necessary for the purposes of those proceedings [AMLR, Article 77(1)].

If a fintech firm decides to terminate a business relationship with a customer due to concerns about the reliability of their identity documents, what specific records must be maintained to ensure compliance with the due diligence requirements, and how should those records be updated if the customer's situation changes later?

The fintech firm must maintain records of the decisions taken regarding the termination of the business relationship, including the relevant supporting documents and justifications, as required under [AMLR, Article 21(3)]. These records must also include documentation of the customer due diligence measures applied, such as the assessment of the reliability of the identity documents, in accordance with [AMLR, Article 20(1)]. If the customer's situation changes later, the firm shall update the due diligence information for the customer on a regular basis or when new risks emerge, as specified in [AMLR, Article 21(3)]. This ensures ongoing compliance with customer due diligence obligations.

If a critical ICT third-party service provider in a non-EU country is designated as critical, and we haven’t yet seen a subsidiary established by that provider within the EU, what steps should we take to ensure our use of their services remains compliant with the relevant rule?

Financial entities shall only make use of the services of an ICT third-party service provider established in a third country and which has been designated as critical if the latter has established a subsidiary in the Union within the 12 months following the designation [DORA, Article 31(12)]. If no such subsidiary has been established within that timeframe, the use of the services of the critical ICT third-party service provider would not comply with the relevant rule [DORA, Article 31(12)]. Therefore, the financial entity must refrain from using the services until the provider establishes a subsidiary in the Union within the 12-month period following designation. This requirement ensures that the provider has a local presence in the Union, thereby enabling effective supervision and compliance with Union data protection and operational resilience standards [DORA, Article 31(12)].

If a fintech firm provides ICT services to another financial entity within the same group, does that mean we are exempt from designating that service provider as a critical ICT third-party service provider under the rules?

No, the exemption from designating a service provider as critical does not apply if the service provider provides ICT services to another financial entity within the same group. The rules explicitly exclude ICT intra-group service providers from the designation of critical ICT third-party service providers [DORA, Article 31(8)]. This exclusion is specifically stated in point (iii) of the list in Article 31(8), which identifies ICT intra-group service providers as being outside the scope of designation [DORA, Article 31(8)]. Therefore, such intra-group arrangements are not subject to the designation process under DORA.

In a scenario where a fintech firm's legal advisor is advising a client on structuring a transaction to avoid detection in a cross-border payment, and the client has disclosed that the funds are being used to facilitate a suspicious financial activity—such as concealing the source of funds—does the exemption in this provision apply, and under what conditions would the advisor be required to report suspicions to the relevant authorities despite being an exempted professional?

The exemption in Article 70(2) of the AMLR does not apply when the legal advisor provides advice for the purposes of money laundering, its predicate offences or terrorist financing, or when the advisor knows that the client is seeking legal advice for such purposes [AMLR, Article 70(2)]. In the scenario described, where the client has disclosed that the funds are being used to conceal the source of funds, this constitutes a clear indication that the legal advice is being sought for the purposes of money laundering [AMLR, Article 70(2)]. Therefore, the advisor is not exempt and must report the suspicion to the relevant authorities, as the advisor's involvement in such activities falls under the conditions specified in subparagraphs (b) and (c) of Article 70(2) [AMLR, Article 70(2)]. This obligation arises regardless of whether the advice is provided before, during, or after judicial proceedings [AMLR, Article 70(2)].

If a fintech firm wants to offer payment initiation services to consumers through a third-party provider, what specific activities must the service provider be authorized to perform under the applicable rules, and what happens if the provider attempts to conduct an activity that is not listed in the authorized activities?

Under PSD2, Article 32(4), Member States may provide that any natural or legal person registered in accordance with paragraph 1 of this Article may engage only in certain activities listed in Article 18. Therefore, the service provider must be authorized to perform only the activities explicitly listed in Article 18 of PSD2. If a third country has been identified as having significant strategic deficiencies in its legal and institutional anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing framework, and those deficiencies are of a persistent nature with no corrective actions taken, the Commission must adopt delegated acts within 20 calendar days of ascertaining that the criteria in point (a), (b), or (c) of Article 29(2) are met [AMLR, Article 29(2)]. Once such delegated acts are adopted, a Member State may require obliged entities established in its territory to apply specific additional countermeasures to mitigate the specific risks stemming from that third country [AMLR, Article 29(6)]. These risks and corresponding countermeasures must be notified to the Commission within five days of being applied [AMLR, Article 29(6)]. The Commission’s assessment must also take into account evaluations, assessments, reports, or public statements by international organisations or standard setters with competence in preventing money laundering and combating terrorist financing [AMLR, Article 29(3)].

The obligation to report compliance issues, including those related to customer authentication and security, falls under the jurisdiction of the host Member State’s competent authorities [PSD2, Article 100(4)].

You must establish, by written agreement, the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance based on the generally acknowledged state of the art, to enable full compliance with the obligations set out in the AI Act, as required for third parties supplying AI systems used in high-risk AI systems [AI Act, Article 25(4)]. This includes ensuring transparency, technical access, and accountability as part of the contractual framework [AI Act, Article 25(4)]. If the third party offers a general-purpose AI model under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters and model architecture, the obligation under Article 53(2) and Article 54(6) does not apply, provided the model does not present systemic risks [AI Act, Article 53(2)]; however, if the model presents systemic risks, the obligations still apply [AI Act, Article 53(2)]. Therefore, in such cases, the fintech platform must still ensure compliance with transparency and accountability requirements through the contractual arrangements with the third party [AI Act, Article 25(4)].

If a third-party cloud service provider refuses to allow a regulatory inspection, the Lead Overseer shall inform the provider of the consequences of such opposition, including the possibility for competent authorities of the relevant financial entities to require financial entities to terminate the contractual arrangements concluded with that critical ICT third-party service provider [DORA, Article 39(7)]. Yes, if the firm is a digital payment service provider regulated under EU financial services law and already has a governance framework that covers internal governance, arrangements, or processes, including risk management and internal controls, then the obligation to establish a quality management system under the AI Act is deemed fulfilled by compliance with those existing requirements [AI Act, Article 17(4)]. The existing governance framework, including risk management and internal controls, may be considered equivalent to the quality management system required under the AI Act [AI Act, Article 9(10)]. Furthermore, the AI Act allows for integration of relevant aspects of the quality management system into existing internal governance arrangements, provided that it achieves an equivalent level of protection [AI Act, Article 17(4)].

If a customer requests access to their personal data and our system indicates that we cannot provide it due to technical limitations, we must inform the customer without delay and at the latest within one month of receipt of the request of the reasons for not taking action [GDPR, Article 12(4)]. The supervisory authority of the complainant, upon adopting the decision for the part concerning dismissal or rejection of the complaint, shall notify the complainant and inform the controller or processor thereof [GDPR, Article 60(9)]. This ensures that the controller is properly informed when the complaint is dismissed, as required by the procedural rules in Article 60(9) [GDPR, Article 60(9)].

In a cross-border payment transaction involving two EU-based fintech firms, if one firm needs to share sensitive customer data with the other to process a transaction, under what conditions can this information be disclosed without violating the rules on professional secrecy and data protection?

The disclosure of sensitive customer data between two EU-based fintech firms in a cross-border payment transaction is permitted under the AMLR, Article 73(5), provided that the firms are located in the Union and the information shared is subject to professional secrecy and personal data protection requirements equivalent to those laid down in the regulation [AMLR, Article 73(5)]. Such disclosure must also comply with the conditions set out in AMLR, Article 75(4), which require that information sharing occurs only for customers at higher risk of money laundering or terrorist financing, and that the information is assessed independently by each obliged entity before any decision affecting the customer is made [AMLR, Article 75(4)]. Additionally, a data protection impact assessment must be carried out prior to processing any personal data, ensuring compliance with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 [AMLR, Article 75(4)]. The sharing of information must also be limited to what is necessary for the performance of their supervisory or compliance tasks under relevant Union or national law [AMLR, Article 75(4)]. Furthermore, if artificial intelligence or machine learning is used, there must be adequate human oversight over the processes generating the information [AMLR, Article 75(4)].

The training data sets used for high-risk AI systems must meet the quality criteria referred to in paragraphs 2 to 5 of Article 10(1) of the AI Act whenever such data sets are used [AI Act, Article 10(1)]. These quality criteria ensure that the data is reliable, representative, and suitable for the intended purpose of the AI system [AI Act, Article 10(1)]. The specific technical and methodological standards for data quality are detailed in those paragraphs, which are part of the broader framework for data governance in high-risk AI systems [AI Act, Article 10(1)]. Additionally, the quality management system under Article 17(1)(f) requires systems and procedures for data management, including data acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, and retention, all of which must be systematically implemented [AI Act, Article 17(1)].

If our system experiences a major outage due to a cyberattack, what steps must we take to ensure our ICT risk management framework remains compliant and up to date, including how we should respond to the supervisory authority's request for a report?

If our system experiences a major outage due to a cyberattack, we must review and update our ICT risk management framework at least once a year or upon the occurrence of such a major ICT-related incident, as required by [DORA, Article 6(5)]. The framework must be continuously improved based on lessons derived from implementation and monitoring, including the incident response and its impact [DORA, Article 6(5)]. In response to the supervisory authority's request, we must submit a report on the review of the ICT risk management framework, as mandated by [DORA, Article 6(5)]. This report should reflect the incident's impact, the effectiveness of preventive measures, and the updated resilience strategies in place [DORA, Article 6(8)].

The platform connecting small insurance intermediaries with local providers falls outside the scope of DORA if the intermediaries are classified as microenterprises, as such intermediaries are explicitly exempted under DORA, Article 2(3), point (e)[DORA, Article 2(3)]. To ensure that the exemption for small, automated transfers without identity verification is not exploited for money laundering or fraud, the platform must implement risk-based monitoring activities as required by [AMLR, Article 6(6)]. This includes establishing internal policies and controls to assess the risk of money laundering and terrorist financing associated with such transactions, as mandated by [AMLR, Article 40(1)]. The platform should apply mitigating measures, such as requiring additional information on the origin and destination of transfers or conducting enhanced ongoing monitoring, particularly for transactions involving self-hosted addresses [AMLR, Article 40(1)]. These measures collectively ensure that the exemption is not abused and that risks are adequately managed.

If we’re transferring personal data from the EU to a country that has been deemed to have an adequate level of protection under an adequacy decision, what steps should we take to ensure that the data transfer remains compliant—especially if there are new developments in the data protection regime of that country after the decision was issued?

If personal data is transferred from the EU to a country that has been deemed to have an adequate level of protection under an adequacy decision, the transfer does not require any specific authorisation [GDPR, Article 45(1)]. However, the Commission’s adequacy decision includes a mechanism for periodic review, at least every four years, which takes into account all relevant developments in the third country or international organisation [GDPR, Article 45(3)]. Therefore, to ensure continued compliance in the face of new developments, the controller must ensure that the adequacy decision remains valid and that the periodic review process has been followed [GDPR, Article 45(3)]. If new developments significantly affect the level of protection, the controller should monitor the situation and, if necessary, seek updated information from the Commission or the relevant supervisory authority [GDPR, Article 45(2)]. The Commission publishes a list of third countries and sectors for which an adequacy decision is in force, which can be used to verify the current status of protection [GDPR, Article 45(8)].
